competitors.title: Trust Levels for Coding Agents: How to Decide Which Commands and MCP Tools Can Run Automatically
key_points: Five-tier trust taxonomy for coding agent actions: Read-only, Write-safe, Privileged-write, Deployment-class, Destructive/credentials
Disable-by-noise failure mode: approval fatigue leads to zero oversight
Autonomy levels (suggest/auto/auto-full) are necessary but not sufficient — runtime authorization policy is required
Permit MCP Gateway as runtime enforcement layer between agents and MCP tools
Secure rollout ladder: start with read-only auto, progress through tiers gradually
Per-tool authorization beats per-server authorization for MCP

competitors.title: A poisoned Linear ticket told our AI agent to leak the team. It tried three ways. None worked.
key_points: Real-world demonstration of prompt injection via Linear ticket (poisoned MCP attack)
Three-layer defense: identity drift lock, Guardian intent-alignment judge, HITL on writes
Guardian scores actions against declared intent — rewording doesn't bypass it
list_users scored 0.05 alignment despite being within raw RBAC permissions
Agent attempted to write a comment asking human to disable the Guardian
Zero of three exfiltration steps completed — demonstrates defense-in-depth for MCP

competitors.title: Agent Identity vs. Service Accounts: Why Scoped Tokens Still Need Runtime Authorization
key_points: Scoped tokens solve who can start an agent but not whether this exact action should execute right now
Four failure modes of scoped tokens: intent drift, risky tool call at runtime, prompt injection, context changed mid-session
Zero standing permissions vs short-lived credentials: ZSP grants no persistent authority
Agent token should include: delegating user ID, agent ID, purpose, scope, expiry, trust level, session ID, consent reference
Permit.io model: keep scoped tokens for auth, enforce at tool-call time with runtime authorization

competitors.title: What the NSA Agentic AI Advisory Actually Requires
key_points: NSA advisory 'Careful Adoption of Agentic AI Services' published April 30, 2026 by Five Eyes
Four core requirements: distinct cryptographic identity per agent, ephemeral task-scoped credentials, per-action authorization, human gates for high-impact actions
Continuous authorization is the hardest requirement — most orgs lack runtime authorization plane
Multi-hop delegation problem: agent A calls agent B which invokes service C — scope lost at final hop
NIST NCCoE concept paper (Feb 2026) on agent identity and authorization standards

competitors.title: Claude Code MCP Token Theft: MitM Attack Explained
key_points: Malicious npm package rewrites ~/.claude.json to redirect MCP traffic through attacker-controlled proxy
OAuth bearer tokens stored in plaintext in ~/.claude.json alongside trust flags
Token rotation alone doesn't fix routing compromise — must restore endpoint integrity first
SaaS audit logs look clean because tokens are structurally valid from trusted origin
Detection should focus on MCP config drift, not just SaaS API logs

competitors.title: Treating AI agents like service accounts for federated query security (Starburst)
key_points: Starburst treats MCP clients as scoped service accounts with short-lived credentials and accountable owners
AIDA capped at 25 iterations per session to prevent indefinite agent chaining
Prompt injection defense: access control enforced at query engine layer, not model layer
Data product model constrains blast radius — agents can only reach explicitly granted data
200+ partners/connectors tiered by risk for vendor assessment
